tagline: An AND-logic-gate engineered probiotic that senses oxidative stress in space and produces vitamin B2 and trehalose to protect astronauts
summary: BNDS-China built OrbitColi, an engineered E. coli probiotic designed to sense oxidative conditions arising from cosmic radiation and microgravity and respond by producing vitamin B2 and trehalose, replacing fixed-dose supplements that degrade over multi-year missions. The scientific framing is quantitative: ISS crews receive 100-200 mSv per year against a 20 mSv occupational limit, and a three-year Mars round trip may accumulate 300-450 mSv. The team's distinguishing contribution is methodological: they invented and applied a five-step education framework, R.E.A.C.H. (Recognize, Experience, Apply, Communicate, Harvest), to every single outreach activity, with a pre-event diagnostic survey and a matched post-event survey, and they report their own failures against it. Integrated Human Practices used a parallel STAR framework (Scan, Test, Assemble, Reflect) across five cycles.

dry.frameworks: Two self-designed frameworks, both documented and reusable: R.E.A.C.H. for education (Recognize the audience's pre-existing attitudes before teaching; Experience through interactive formats; Apply by moving the audience from listeners to designers; Communicate to close the loop by harvesting informed project feedback into Integrated Human Practices; Harvest by quantifying the event's success and planning the next iteration) and STAR for iHP (Scan, Test, Assemble, Reflect) across five cycles: problem validation, end-user and market needs, technical design, biosafety and ethics, and production and final-product development. The REACH structure is published in detailed appendices so other teams can reuse it.
dry.dataviz: Before-and-after bar charts of self-reported technique familiarity and interest; questionnaire-result figures published for each activity (pre and post); a timeline figure of all educational activities; pre-interview and final stakeholder influence/relevance maps for iHP, with the honest caveat printed on the figure that inclusion in the pre-interview map does not mean an interview took place.
dry.datascience: Systematic paired pre/post surveying with reported N and percentages, e.g. kindergarten cohort N = 14 matched responses, 21 student athletes aged 10-13 surveyed before and after, 16 valid responses per question from the elderly session, eight older adults aged 68-82 interviewed at the scoping stage, and two school-wide perception surveys on synthetic biology and on attitudes to engineered-bacteria consumption and space microbial applications, all published as downloadable files.
dry.software: The project includes hardware and software components presented to audiences for feedback; the team learned an AI protein-design workflow from team NBJF (generate structure, fill amino-acid sequence, in-silico screening, wet-lab validation) and explicitly reserved wet-lab capacity because high in-silico scores can lose function in reality.
stack: downloadable lesson slide decks and protocols
techniques: protein thermal and radiation resistance engineering

good.publicEngagement: BNDS-China's practice is distinctive because every activity is written up against the same five-step template, R.E.A.C.H., which forces a pre-event diagnostic, an interactive delivery, a design task, a project-feedback loop and a quantified post-event evaluation - and the team reports honestly where a step was skipped. The highest-value example is a kindergarten programme for pre-literate 5-6 year olds. The Recognize step established through a pre-event survey that children already saw microbes as invisible enemies (hand-washing framing) and that 71.43% preferred interactive games to lectures. The team then rendered BioBrick standard assembly as a colour-coded tactile block system: a blue 'switch' promoter block that must come first, a red 'function' coding-sequence block compared to a light bulb, a yellow 'stop' terminator block compared to a vehicle brake, and a green 'little house' vector and chassis block, with assembly order taught as a chanted mantra ('Flip open the blue switch, let the red function bloom, halt with the yellow brake, and live inside the green room!'). Children worked in pairs and trios called 'syndicates' with visual challenge cards posing local problems (make plants glow to light a path to a playground at night; make a flower that masks the smell of garbage). The cleverest design move: the team deliberately rationed parts, giving one table switches but no coding blocks and the next table the reverse, so children had to discover what they lacked, approach other groups and barter - a lived introduction to the open-source iGEM Registry. A five-act puppet show, 'Microscopic Defense Line', dramatised a grazed arm at cell scale, and deliberately avoided weapons or war imagery: the White Blood Cell puppet hugged the bacterium to represent phagocytosis, two red blood cell actors held hands to bridge a vessel, and platelet actors pressed yellow paper against stretchy cloth to show clotting. Measured results from matched surveys (N = 14): before, 78.57% did not know what it meant to pass a function from one organism to another and 64.29% did not know or only vaguely knew what a gene is; after, 92.86% described synthetic biology as 'building blocks', 92.86% knew the promoter starts expression and 100% knew the coding sequence determines function; 42.86% had thought the body fights invaders like 'little soldiers' and none knew clots form, versus 100% afterwards understanding both white blood cell clearance and platelet repair; 100% enjoyed the activities and 92.86% wanted more science stories. The feedback even changed the project: children asked why immune clearance has to kill ('Can't they just change them? Make them friends?') and worried what happens if the yellow stop block falls off, which the team mapped onto transcriptional runaway, biocontainment and biocontamination and used to question their own antagonistic-clearance therapeutic model. Other formats, each with REACH write-ups: a BioCamp lecture on the whole molecular toolkit (PCR, gel electrophoresis, Southern/Northern/Western blotting, qPCR, rtPCR, FISH, CRISPR-Cas9, gene circuits) where each technique was framed by the question it answers, with the team candidly recording that the Apply and Communicate steps did not happen and that students still found the techniques complicated without hands-on work, and publishing the fix (fewer techniques per session, add pipetting and gel loading, one workflow diagram); a formal debate on 9 March 2026 with the BNDS British Debate Club on whether synthetic biology should modify human traits unrelated to serious disease, supported by a purpose-written Synthetic Bio Debate Information Packet covering definitions, design principles, systems thinking, intervention targets, risks, ethics and governance, with pre- and post-debate questionnaires; a campus art exhibition on environmental protection with a pop-art digital painting and an explanatory signboard, made with a visual-arts student, where the recorded criticism was that the symbols were too abstract; a bilingual comic published in the school newspaper BNDS Review and released as downloadable Chinese and English digital versions; and merchandise-as-conversation-starter at the Hongchuanghui Fair and school carnival, with original E. coli, yeast and budding-yeast cartoon designs on postcards, stickers and acrylic hair clips, where the team explicitly explained which features were biological and which were artistic licence. The inclusivity work is specific about barriers. At Tianyun Rehabilitation Center in Liulihe, Fangshan District, Beijing, working with hearing-impaired children and children with genetic conditions, the team discovered the children had no independent electronic devices and that a conventional questionnaire did not suit their communication needs, so after consulting the centre's teachers they switched to an illustrated storybook, 'Little Chef Mimi and Her Magical Yeast Friends', plus a colouring activity, and relied on the teachers to interpret the children's sign language - concluding that inclusive science education is about making sure every child's voice can be heard, not just making knowledge easier. For children with osteogenesis imperfecta ('porcelain doll' patients), the team first interviewed directors of the Sun and Rain Center rare-disease organisation, who explicitly advised against treating participants as fragile or showing pity; sessions were kept short, and when the team noticed holding pens was physically hard for some children, they abandoned the planned drawing activity mid-session for an open discussion and a 'wishing' segment, then shifted their long-term approach to accessible online workshops and distributing game materials directly to hospitals. For 21 student athletes aged 10-13 with limited access to systematic biology teaching or lab equipment, three experiments (strawberry DNA extraction, saliva pH around exercise, ruler-drop reaction tests) tied biology to their own bodies; afterwards all 21 reported confidence in understanding and completing experiments and all answered the DNA and synthetic-biology questions correctly. A lecture for older adults, built on scoping interviews with eight people aged 68-82 whose concerns were medical safety, side effects and the reliability of health information, used genetically modified food, vaccines and microbial insulin as familiar anchors, taught how to spot misleading health advertising and how AI can help check claims, and included making DNA-themed bracelets and illustrated tote bags carrying health-scam reminders; of 16 post-event responses, 15 (93.75%) rejected a misleading miracle-product claim, all 16 answered the GM food, vaccine, insulin and AI-checking items as intended, 81.25% found explanations easy to understand and 87.5% called the activity very helpful.
good.ihp: Five iHP cycles (problem validation, end-user and market needs, technical design, biosafety and ethics, production and final product) were each run through the team's STAR loop. A pre-interview stakeholder map linked each cycle to the expert groups whose input it needed, and a final map recorded each stakeholder's influence on the project and the project's relevance to them. The team documented a hard limit transparently: regulatory restrictions prevented them from interviewing astronauts or national regulatory authorities. Aerospace food and nutrition experts defined the nutritional context; space medicine and clinical experts shaped the health-need and biosafety assessment. Education fed directly back into design, most notably the kindergarten children's biocontainment and mutualism questions. A cross-team exchange with team NBJF on AI protein design taught the team to compartmentalise the workflow and to avoid over-reliance on in-silico prediction, and they adopted NBJF's 'phenomenon-first, jargon-later' principle for explaining their AND logic-gate probiotic to lay audiences.
good.realWorld: The project targets a documented gap in astronaut health protection: pre-packaged vitamins and antioxidants provide fixed dosing that cannot track real-time biochemical change, and shelf-life degradation makes them unreliable over multi-year missions. Education outputs were deliberately packaged for reuse: an openly available children's book, downloadable comic in Chinese and English, the debate information packet, lecture slide decks, bilingual activity PowerPoints, the strawberry DNA extraction protocol, and detailed REACH appendices so other teams and educators can replicate the structure rather than just the activities.

gemsTakeaway: Adopt a single named template for every outreach event - BNDS-China's R.E.A.C.H. (Recognize with a pre-event diagnostic, Experience, Apply, Communicate project feedback back into design, Harvest with a matched post-event survey) - and publish the results including the steps you failed to complete; the paired pre/post numbers and the honest gaps are what turn a scrapbook of events into evidence.
